About This Part
Volume 7E develops the enterprise control plane around Azure workloads. Earlier parts established identity,
infrastructure, data platforms, containers, serverless compute, and integration. This part turns those
capabilities into an operable cloud platform through declarative delivery, secure pipelines, telemetry, policy,
threat detection, incident response, landing-zone governance, resilience engineering, and cost accountability. The goal is not to memorize product blades. It is to build a repeatable operating model in which every change is
reviewed, every deployment is traceable, every workload is observable, every privilege is bounded, every
control produces evidence, and every recovery procedure is tested. Safety, Security, and Cost Controls

Use sandbox subscriptions, budgets, owner tags, expiry dates, and approved regions before provisioning
labs.

Use workload identity federation, managed identities, and short-lived credentials. Do not store client
secrets, publish profiles, PATs, or access keys in repositories or pipeline variables.

Treat policy exemptions, break-glass access, security suppressions, firewall changes, and release overrides
as time-bound, owned, and auditable.

Filter sensitive telemetry, minimize retention, and avoid placing credentials, tokens, personal data, or
regulated payloads in logs and traces.

Use synthetic data and controlled test systems. Do not run destructive deployment-stack, policy-
remediation, failover, or incident-response exercises in production.


Chapter 41 - Azure Resource Manager, Bicep, and Deployment
Stacks
Designing deterministic Azure infrastructure lifecycle with modular Bicep, safe change review, deployment stacks,
and policy-aware automation
Learning Objectives

Explain ARM control-plane behavior, scopes, idempotent declarations, dependency resolution, and
deployment history.

Build reusable Bicep modules with typed parameters, outputs, validation, and secure defaults.

Use what-if, deployment stacks, locks, policy, and staged rollouts to reduce destructive change risk.

Troubleshoot authorization, provider registration, quota, policy, dependency, and lifecycle errors.
41.1 Declarative Infrastructure and the ARM Control Plane
Azure Resource Manager is the control plane through which Azure resources are created, updated, tagged,
locked, and deleted. Bicep is a domain-specific language that compiles to ARM JSON while providing a cleaner
authoring experience. A production design separates desired state, environment parameters, policy,
deployment identity, and operational evidence.

Keep resource names, locations, SKU choices, network exposure, identities, diagnostic settings, tags, and
locks explicit.

Deploy at the narrowest appropriate scope: resource group, subscription, management group, or tenant.

Treat outputs as contracts between modules, not as a place to expose secrets.

Use modules for stable capabilities such as networking, monitoring, identity, and application landing zones.

A module should have a clear owner, semantic version, compatibility notes, tests, examples, policy expectations,
and upgrade path. Pin module versions and provider API versions intentionally. Record source revision, module

deployment validation.

identity.

Avoid implicit cross-resource assumptions. Model dependencies and output contracts explicitly.

Use a controlled module registry or template spec and scan source before publication.

Test rollback as a forward corrective deployment; ARM does not provide a universal transactional rollback. Troubleshooting Matrix

1. Why use Bicep instead of raw ARM JSON?
Bicep provides concise syntax, type safety, modules, tooling, and the same ARM capabilities because it
compiles to ARM JSON.
2. What problem do deployment stacks solve?
They track a managed set of resources and support explicit lifecycle and deny settings beyond ordinary
deployment history.
3. Why is what-if not sufficient by itself?
It is a critical preview, but production safety also requires policy evaluation, ownership, data-impact review,
approvals, tests, and post-deployment validation.
4. How do you roll back an infrastructure deployment?
Prefer a reviewed forward fix or redeployment of a known-good declaration; separately protect and restore
stateful data when required. Chapter Summary

Use Bicep modules and narrow scopes to create deterministic declarations.

Review every change with what-if and policy-aware gates.

Use deployment stacks carefully for resource lifecycle, not as an excuse for broad deletion.

Preserve complete release and validation evidence.

Measure lead time to first compliant environment, deployment success, golden-path adoption, exception

number of templates. A good platform makes the safe path faster than a custom path.

A supported, automated path with secure defaults, documentation, observability, and clear ownership that

Both distribute reusable declarations; template specs are ARM resources for versioned templates, while a

Developer lead time, successful adoption, platform reliability, exception demand, support load, cost, and user

Chapter 43 - Azure DevOps Organizations, Repos, Boards, and
Artifacts
Designing traceable engineering work, repository governance, package provenance, access boundaries, and
lifecycle controls
Learning Objectives

Structure Azure DevOps organizations and projects around ownership and isolation requirements.

Configure repository protections, branch policies, identity scopes, and secret prevention.

Connect work items, commits, builds, packages, releases, incidents, and evidence.

Operate Azure Artifacts feeds with provenance, retention, upstream-source, and permission controls.
43.1 Organization and Project Boundaries
An Azure DevOps organization is a major administrative and identity boundary. Projects organize repositories,
pipelines, boards, feeds, teams, and permissions. Avoid one project per microservice without reason, but also
avoid a single project that allows unrelated teams to inherit broad access.

Use Microsoft Entra groups for membership and lifecycle. Avoid individual permissions where possible.

Separate administrators, service identities, contributors, readers, auditors, and external collaborators.

Enable least-privilege job authorization scope and restrict cross-project repository access.

Review inactive users, PATs, OAuth grants, service hooks, extensions, agents, and service connections.
43.2 Repository and Branch Governance
Production repositories require reviewed changes, build validation, resolved comments, linked work,
appropriate reviewer independence, and controlled bypass. Protect default branches and release tags. Do not
treat branch policy as a substitute for secure build identity and artifact verification.

Interview Questions and Model Answers
1. How should Azure DevOps projects be bounded?
By ownership, lifecycle, compliance, isolation, and collaboration needs rather than a fixed one-project-per-
service rule.
2. Why limit job authorization scope?
It reduces the blast radius of a compromised pipeline by preventing automatic access to unrelated projects
and repositories.
3. Why promote packages instead of rebuilding?
Promotion preserves artifact identity and proves the tested package is the one released.
4. What makes a release traceable?
A chain from requirement and source revision through build, tests, artifact identity, approvals, deployment,
telemetry, and incidents. Chapter Summary

Design organization and project boundaries around least privilege and ownership.

Protect repositories with independent review and trusted validation.

Use immutable package versions and controlled promotion.

Connect work, source, artifacts, releases, and operations end to end.

Chapter 44 - Azure Pipelines Continuous Integration and Agent
Security
Building reproducible, isolated, credential-free CI systems with trusted templates, ephemeral agents, quality gates,
and supply-chain evidence
Learning Objectives

Design YAML pipelines with stages, templates, parameters, conditions, and deterministic artifacts.

Secure Microsoft-hosted and self-hosted agents against untrusted code and credential theft.

Use workload identity federation and scoped pipeline identities instead of stored cloud secrets.

Produce tests, SBOMs, provenance, scan results, and immutable packages as CI evidence.
44.1 CI Architecture and Template Governance
A continuous-integration pipeline converts reviewed source into a verified, immutable artifact. YAML belongs
in source control, but reusable security-critical logic should be centralized in protected templates. Separate
compile/test/package from deployment. A build must be reproducible from the recorded source revision and
dependency lock files.

private networks, specialized tools, or large builds, but require patching, isolation, image management, egress
control, secret cleanup, capacity, and incident procedures.

where possible. The pipeline receives a short-lived token through OIDC instead of storing a client secret. Scope

Sign artifacts or produce verifiable provenance where the delivery system supports it.

1. Why prefer workload identity federation?
It exchanges an OIDC assertion for short-lived Azure credentials and removes stored client-secret rotation
and leakage risk.
2. When are self-hosted agents justified?
When builds need private connectivity, specialized hardware/tooling, or performance not available on hosted
agents, with explicit security ownership.
3. Why separate build and deployment identities?
Compromise of build execution should not automatically grant permission to change production.
4. What evidence should CI produce?
Source revision, dependency and tool versions, tests, scans, SBOM, provenance, artifact digest, and
publication record. Chapter Summary

CI must generate immutable, verified artifacts rather than deploy directly.

Centralize trusted templates and isolate untrusted code.

Use ephemeral agents and workload identity federation.

Preserve supply-chain evidence and reproducibility.
